items.readable_text:
Content:
Fraction multiplication can often be interpreted as the area of a part of a unit square.

Content:
Let's consider the unit square below. It has sides of length [MATH: 1] unit, divided into lots of little tiles.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/7b1a8f2f48c909e8319f2319fd5f6344]

Content:
Each side of the unit square is divided into [MATH: \color{blue}4] equal pieces. So, each side of a tile is [MATH: \dfrac{1}{\color{blue}4}] units long.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/36e3503a5a0e8c93a90ecf313a2c2a43]

Content:
The area of each tile is the product of the two side lengths. Therefore, the area of each tile is
[MATH: \dfrac{1}{4} \times \dfrac{1}{4}\;\textrm{square units}.]

Content:
Another way of computing the area of a part of a unit square is to realize that we can find the area of a single tile using the following formula:

Content:
[MATH: \textrm{area of a single tile} = \dfrac{1}{\textrm{number of tiles}}.]

Content:
Knowing this, what is the area of the shaded region below, in square units?

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/8df1dffcd02ba30d75540506ef65101c]

Content:
First, note that the region is [MATH: 7] tiles long and [MATH: 7] tiles high.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/e95db5ab9215bc444f8f355e3cfac7f1]

Content:
So there are a total of [MATH: 7 \times 7 = 49] small square tiles. Therefore, the area of each tile is [MATH: \dfrac{1}{49}] square units.

Content:
Since [MATH: 10] tiles are shaded, the total shaded area is:

Content:
[MATH: 10\times\dfrac{1}{49} = \dfrac{10}{49} \,\textrm{square units}.]

Another way of computing the area of a part of a unit square is to realize that we can find the area of a single tile using the following formula:
